De kwetsbaarheden bevinden zich in de API-endpoints van Omnissa Workspace ONE UEM. De eerste kwetsbaarheid stelt kwaadwillenden in staat om ongeautoriseerde toegang te krijgen tot gevoelige informatie met behulp van de Path Traversal-techniek. Dit kan leiden tot het ophalen van vertrouwelijke gegevens. De tweede kwetsbaarheid betreft een Server-Side Request Forgery (SSRF) die ook ongeautoriseerde toegang tot gevoelige interne systeeminformatie mogelijk maakt en de mogelijkheid biedt om interne netwerkbronnen te enumereren. Oplossingen Omnissa heeft updates uitgebracht om de kwetsbaarheden te verhelpen en adviseert te updaten naar versies gelijk aan of hoger dan 24.10.0.11, 24.6.0.35, 24.2.0.30 of 23.10.0.50. documents.title: Microsoft Copilot Chat Privacy and Protections | Microsoft Learn
documents.text: Microsoft Copilot Chat Privacy and Protections | Microsoft Learn Microsoft 365 Copilot Chat protects workplace AI-powered web chats by providing enterprise data protection to keep organizations safe. Learn about the data protections, authentication, authorization, and GDPR compliance. Skip to main content Table of contents Exit editor mode Reading mode Table of contents Add Copy Markdown Print Privacy and protections Summarize this article for me In this article Note Microsoft 365 Copilot is now named Microsoft Copilot, and Microsoft 365 Copilot Chat is now named Microsoft Copilot Chat. Some experiences, licenses, and capabilities might continue to reference Microsoft 365 Copilot and Microsoft 365 Copilot Chat during the transition period. There are no changes to security, compliance, and privacy for organizations. Microsoft Copilot Chat prompts and responses are processed within the Microsoft 365 service boundary, which offers enterprise data protection . This means that security, privacy, and compliance controls and commitments available for Microsoft Copilot also extend to Copilot Chat. Prompts and responses aren't used to train the underlying foundation models. Prompt: User selects a prewritten prompt or writes their own prompt in Copilot Chat from the web, the Microsoft Copilot app, Teams, or Outlook. The prompt is sent to the Copilot orchestrator for processing. Copilot Chat uses the same orchestrator as Microsoft Copilot to process prompts and responses. It coordinates Responsible AI (RAI) safety checks throughout the process and logs the interaction for auditing/eDiscovery. The specific controls and policies vary depending on the underlying subscription plan. Grounding: Copilot preprocesses the input prompt using web grounding via the Bing search service (only applicable if web grounding is enabled). Web grounding sends web search queries consisting of a few words generated from the prompt to Bing to provide relevant information for the response. Queries are sent via a secure connection to Bing and don't include any user or tenant identifiers. Additional contractual protections apply to these queries when sent to Bing. For more information on web search queries, see Privacy and security for generated search queries . Unlike Microsoft Copilot, Copilot Chat is not grounded in organizational content like files, emails, or chats as part of the chat experience—it is grounded in data from the web only. If Copilot Chat users would like to use organizational content in their chat, they can do so in four ways: As part of their prompt (such as copying and pasting in content, uploading a file using the '+' button, dragging and dropping a file into the chat box, including a file by typing '/' and selecting it from the ContextIQ menu, or selecting a suggested prompt which contains a file). By using Copilot Chat in Outlook. In this scenario, Copilot Chat can access user data including their emails, calendar, meetings, chats, and limited file content (OneDrive and SharePoint). By using a pay-as-you-go agent that has access to organizational content. Learn more about organizational data and Copilot Chat (within this article). Large Language Model (LLM): Copilot sends the grounded prompt to the LLM to generate a relevant response. Copilot Chat may use multiple models to generate a response. Logging: Before sending the response back to the user, both the prompt and response are logged and stored in Exchange for auditing/eDiscovery (Microsoft 365 tenant). Response: Copilot coordinates Responsible AI (RAI) safety checks and returns the response to the app and the user. The following video provides an overview of privacy, security, and compliance in Copilot Chat. It's 2 minutes and 27 seconds long. Enterprise data protection for prompts and responses Copilot Chat offers enterprise data protection (EDP) for prompts and responses. EDP is available in Copilot Chat at no extra cost. Copilot Chat makes it clear that enterprise data protection is applied by featuring a green shield along the top of the user interface next to the New Chat button. Enterprise data protection refers to controls and commitments, under the Data Protection Addendum (DPA) and the Product Terms , that apply to customer data for users of Microsoft Copilot and Copilot Chat, with Microsoft acting as a data processor. Get more details on enterprise data protection for prompts and responses in Microsoft Copilot and Copilot Chat. Privacy and security of generated search queries To help improve the quality of responses, Copilot Chat can use web search queries sent to the Bing search service to ground responses in the latest information from the web. The Bing search service operates separately from Microsoft 365 and has different data-handling practices from those used for prompts and responses. These data-handling practices are covered by the Microsoft Services Agreement between each user and Microsoft, together with the Microsoft Privacy Statement . This means that Microsoft acts as an independent data controller responsible for complying with all applicable laws and controller obligations. This approach is consistent with other optional connected experiences that rely on Bing . Learn more about data, privacy, and security of web queries . How generated search queries work: Copilot Chat parses a user's prompt and identifies terms where web search would improve the quality of the response. Based on these terms, Copilot Chat generates a search query that it sends via secure connection to the Bing search service asking for more information. This generated search query is different from the user's original prompt—it consists of a few words informed by the user's prompt. Additional terms from uploaded files or content actively viewed in Edge may also be sent to the Bing search service to ground responses if Copilot Chat needs them to understand the user's prompt. The following information is not included in the generated query sent to the Bing search service: Any user or tenant identifiers (for example: username, domain, or tenant ID) The user's entire prompt, unless the prompt is very short (for example, "local weather") Entire files uploaded into Copilot Chat (uploaded files are stored in a user's OneDrive for Business as part of enterprise data protection) Entire web pages or PDFs summarized by Copilot Chat in Edge Generated web search queries aren't shared with advertisers. Also, web search queries sent to Bing don't impact any of the following: Search ranking Answers or features like rich captions Social features like autosuggest, trending, and zero input After Copilot Chat receives additional information from the Bing search service, this information is used to compose the response returned to the user. This table provides examples of a user's prompt and the generated search queries sent to Bing. It also explains how Copilot Chat formulates a response. User prompt Generated search queries How Copilot Chat provides a response We're considering a possible acquisition of Fabrikam. Summarize financial information about the company, including their business strategy. Fabrikam strategy Fabrikam financials Copilot Chat returns a response that includes publicly available information relevant to these two search queries. Along with the prompt, the user uploads a document about clean energy strategy. Summarize this document and tell me if Fabrikam has publicly announced a similar approach. Fabrikam clean energy policy announcements Copilot Chat reasons over this document and identifies "clean energy policy" as a major theme. "Clean energy policy" is added to the generated search query sent to the Bing search service (the document itself isn't included). The rest of the generated query is inferred from the prompt itself. Copilot Chat then takes web search results returned from Bing and identifies any similarities between this public information and the strategy described in the internal document. After the chat session ends, the document is no longer retained by Copilot Chat. User has navigated to a public news article on the web about clean energy and uses Copilot Chat in Edge to ask for a summary. What does this article say about clean energy? None To generate a page summary, Copilot Chat can infer all needed information from the text on the page itself. No generated search query is necessary. After the chat session ends, any information from the web page is no longer retained by Copilot Chat. Web search query citations To provide greater visibility into the generated search queries, web search query citations are shown to users in the linked citation section of the Copilot Chat response. This section shows the exact web search queries (derived from the user's prompt) that were sent to the Bing search service. Showing the exact web search queries helps users understand what search queries, along with the sites searched, were used to enhance Copilot Chat's response to their prompt. This information can help users improve their prompts and use Copilot Chat more effectively. Web search query citations are available in the chat thread for 24 hours. Logging prompts and responses With enterprise data protection, prompts and responses in Copilot Chat are logged. The same retention policies used for Microsoft Copilot can be used for Copilot Chat. This allows for new feature experiences like allowing users to return to a previous chat. Learn more about retention policies or audit logging . Note The specific controls and policies will vary depending on the underlying subscription plan. Organizational data Copilot Chat is a generative AI service grounded in data from the public web from the Bing search service. Unlike Microsoft Copilot, Copilot Chat can only access organizational content in select circumstances. Users have four options to access content from their organization for Copilot Chat to use: Option 1 – Provide content as part of their prompt: Users can provide organizational content as part of their prompt in Copilot Chat. They can do so in the following ways: Users explicitly type or paste this information directly into the chat. Users upload a file by selecting the '+' button in the chat box. They can also drag and drop a file into the chat box. Uploaded files are stored in a user's OneDrive for Business as part of enterprise data protection. Users type '/' in the prompt box to open the ContextIQ menu and search for a specific file they have access to. This adds the file to the prompt for Copilot Chat to reason over, just as if they had uploaded the file. Users select a suggested prompt from under the prompt box that contains a file that the user has access to. Suggested prompts containing files are shown to the user based on interaction signals (such as if the file was accessed, modified, or shared with or by the user) and file properties (such as when it was created or last updated by the user). Option 2 – Use Copilot Chat with open content: In select scenarios, Copilot Chat is aware of the user's open content which enables Copilot Chat to engage with it. This can happen in the following scenarios: When using the Word, Excel, or PowerPoint agents, Copilot Chat is aware of the user's open content like a file or spreadsheet. This allows users to ask questions, generate content, and otherwise engage with that content while using Copilot Chat. Copilot Chat is only aware of the specific content that the user has open and cannot access other work data unless the user provides it. When using the Microsoft Copilot mobile app and selecting a suggested prompt with a file, Copilot Chat will use the file's content as part of the response. When using Copilot Chat in Edge if the 'Allow access to any webpage or PDF' setting is enabled by the user or admin and an intranet page is open in the browser. In this scenario, Copilot Chat can use the content of this page to help answer questions. Option 3 - Use Copilot Chat in Outlook: Copilot Chat in Outlook can access user data to provide relevant responses. The accessible user data includes their emails, calendar, meetings, chats, and files limited to the following boundaries: Files in a user's OneDrive and other OneDrive files they have access to Files from their frequently visited SharePoint sites Files that were shared directly with them Files that a user has viewed, edited, or created This lets users do things like ask questions about their inbox, prioritize and triage their emails, or prepare for upcoming meetings when using Copilot Chat in Outlook. User data used by Copilot Chat in its response is accessed via lexical indexing. Access to full work data as part of Work IQ and semantic indexing is only available for users with the Microsoft Copilot license. Option 4 – Use an agent that has access to organizational content: Users can also access organizational content through agents that have been grounded in shared tenant data, such as SharePoint or Microsoft 365 Copilot connector content. While using these agents, users can prompt Copilot Chat about the data or content that the agent has access to. Learn more about discovering, creating, or utilizing agents . Copilot Chat does not use your data to train foundation models. Note Chat experiences in Word, Excel, and PowerPoint vary depending on your tenant configuration and license. Learn more in the Microsoft Copilot overview . Generating files in Word, Excel, and PowerPoint agents Copilot Chat allows users to generate files from prompts within the Word, Excel, and PowerPoint agents. PowerPoint presentations generated by Copilot Chat are stored in the user's OneDrive if storage is available. Copilot-generated Word documents and Excel workbooks are available for download by the user. PowerPoint presentations are also available for download if OneDrive storage isn't available. General Data Protection Regulation (GDPR) The May 21, 2018, blog post from Microsoft outlines our commitment to GDPR compliance and how Microsoft helps businesses and other organizations meet their own GDPR obligations. With enterprise data protection, Copilot Chat supports GDPR. Get more details on GDPR when using Microsoft products and services . EU Data Boundary (EUDB) Copilot Chat calls to the LLM are routed to the closest data centers in the region, but can also call into other regions where greater capacity is available when utilization is especially high. For European Union (EU) users, Copilot Chat has additional safeguards to comply with the EU Data Boundary . EU traffic stays within the EU Data Boundary, while worldwide traffic can be sent to the EU and other countries or regions for LLM processing. Copilot Chat data residency commitments are outlined in the Microsoft Product Terms and Data Protection Addendum . Web search queries sent from Copilot Chat to Bing are not EUDB-compliant. See more information on how Microsoft handles generated search queries . Microsoft Copilot is an AI-powered assistant that helps you work more efficiently by generating content, answering questions, analyzing information, and automating tasks. It combines large language models with your work data from Microsoft Graph and Microsoft 365 to provide personalized assistance. Copilot Chat is a web-grounded AI assistant included at no additional cost with eligible Microsoft 365 plans. It also includes Copilot in Outlook and the Microsoft Copilot app. Customers can use custom agents built by their organization on a metered basis. When you purchase a Microsoft 365 plan with Copilot, or add a Microsoft 365 Copilot license to an existing subscription, you unlock additional capabilities, including Work IQ , Copilot in Teams and Microsoft 365 apps such as Word, Excel, and PowerPoint, access to Microsoft pre-built agents like Researcher, Analyst, and Facilitator, and the ability to use assistive custom agents at no additional cost. Organizations with Microsoft 365 Copilot licenses also gain access to advanced analytics to measure usage, adoption, and business impact. 02/ Which apps support Microsoft Copilot and what can it do in each? Copilot delivers AI assistance tailored to the Microsoft 365 apps. For example, in Word, it helps draft documents, suggest edits, and summarize text. In Excel, it analyzes data, creates charts, and generates insights. In PowerPoint, it helps design presentations by generating outlines and recommending images or layouts. In Outlook, it drafts emails and summarizes lengthy email threads. In Teams, it recaps meetings and highlights action items from chats. 03/ What Microsoft Copilot features are usage-based? Everyday AI experiences, like chat and Copilot in your Microsoft 365 apps, are included with your license. More advanced AI experiences are billed based on usage. Today, these include Copilot Cowork, Code, Autopilot, and the Work IQ APIs. More usage-based services may be added over time. 04/ How does usage-based billing work? Usage-based billing lets you pay for advanced AI capabilities based on how much you use them. These experiences use Copilot Credits, so you pay based on actual usage, while the Copilot capabilities included with your subscription stay included. Learn more about usage-based billing and Copilot Credits. Learn more about usage-based billing and Copilot Credits . 05/ How do I control what my organization spends? Administrators can manage usage-based billing in Cost Management in the Microsoft 365 admin center. You can adjust usage controls and spending policies to fit your organization’s needs. Charges apply only when usage-based experiences are used. 06/ Which languages does Microsoft Copilot support? See the list of supported languages . 07/ How does Microsoft Copilot help support data security and privacy? Microsoft Copilot is built with enterprise-grade security and privacy, using the same controls and permissions that help protect your data in Microsoft 365. Copilot follows your organization’s existing Microsoft 365 security settings. With enterprise data protection (EDP) in Copilot, prompts and responses stay within the Microsoft 365 service boundary and all associated data handling commitments apply, including support for General Data Protection Regulation (GDPR ), International Organization for Standardization (ISO )/IEC 27018, and the Microsoft Data Protection Addendum (DPA ). Prompts and responses are logged, subject to your data retention policies, and will be available for eDiscovery and other Microsoft Purview capabilities. The specific controls will vary depending on the underlying subscription plan. Prompts and responses are not used to train the underlying large language models. 08/ What are the main benefits of Microsoft Copilot for business? Microsoft Copilot enhances business processes by combining large language models (LLMs) with your work context. Key features include: Microsoft Graph Grounding and Microsoft Graph connectors: Adds context from emails, chats, documents, and meetings.​ Enterprise Data Protection (EDP): Ensures data stays within Microsoft 365 boundaries, supporting GDPR and other standards.​ Copilot Chat: Integrates web, work, and business data into a rich information database.​ Copilot Pages: Organizes and shares content for easy collaboration and project tracking.​ Copilot in the flow of your work: Available in Microsoft 365 apps like Word, Excel, PowerPoint, and Outlook.​ Microsoft Teams collaboration: Streamlines meetings with real-time summaries and insights.​ Pre-built agents: Connects to business applications, including SharePoint.​ Copilot Studio: Enables users to create and customize workflow agents using the Copilot Chat or Standard harness.​ IT controls: Helps manage AI at scale including management controls, measurement, and reporting. 09/ What is Work IQ and how does it work? Work IQ is the intelligence layer that enriches Microsoft Copilot and agents with an implicit understanding of your work—inside and out. It connects your context, workflows, and relationships to deliver an experience that is built just for you and the flow of your work. Work IQ includes data from multiple sources: Microsoft 365 content and metadata; line of business data ingested through Copilot connectors—and the comprehensive semantic index derived from your Microsoft 365 and line-of-business datasets. Work IQ also includes Copilot Memory to better understand your style, habits, and preferences. The result is a rich experience that is implicitly grounded in the details of your work patterns, relationships, and workflows. It enables Copilot to provide new insights and anticipate future needs and proactively take action to deliver the best results. 10/ What are agents and what can they do? Agents are AI systems that help individuals and organizations manage tasks and make informed decisions. Using agents within Copilot, you and your business can drive efficiency and get more work done faster. Agents can perform various tasks to assist people and organizations: Retrieve information: Query systems like HR, CRM, or financial databases. Help with basic tasks: Submit expense reports, update CRM systems, create IT help desk tickets. Perform specialized roles: Facilitate meetings, compile research reports, analyze data sets. Automate processes: Handle financial planning, sales qualification, and supplier communications. 11/ What’s the difference between Copilot Studio in Microsoft Copilot and Copilot Studio licensed separately? Copilot Studio that’s included with a Microsoft 365 Copilot license lets the licensed users build and use internal agents within Microsoft 365 using the Copilot Chat and Standard harness at no additional cost. The standalone Copilot Studio license offers additional flexibility—you can create agents using the GitHub Copilot harness and publish to external channels (like websites, apps, and social platforms), non-licensed users can use the agent, and you can choose from different pricing options. (Nasdaq: BSP) today announced its results for Q3 2026. Highlights from Q3 2026: Revenue was $780 million, up 125% from Q3 2025. Operating income was $172 million, up 34% from Q3 2025. Adjusted Operating Income¹ was $424 million, up 130% from Q3 2025. Diluted earnings per share was $0.13, down 3% from Q3 2025. Adjusted Earnings per Share² was $0.42, up 98% from Q3 2025. We completed the acquisition of Airtable for an enterprise value of $1.29 billion. Airtable is a collaborative platform where organizations build and run workflows and applications. At the end of the quarter, net debt was $4.00 billion and leverage ratio³ was 2.1×. Cash and cash equivalents totaled $1.02 billion, and we had $2.33 billion of available borrowing capacity under our undrawn committed term loan and revolving credit facilities. Key events that occurred subsequent to the end of Q3 2026: We entered into an agreement to acquire Mailchimp from Intuit for an enterprise value of $3.68 billion. Mailchimp helps millions of businesses plan, execute, and optimize their email marketing campaigns. We completed the acquisition of Miro for an enterprise value of $1.36 billion. Miro supports teams as they brainstorm, plan, and execute projects together. We raised $330 million of gross proceeds through a private placement with Berkshire Hathaway of 10 million ordinary shares of Bending Spoons. We agreed to sell 32.5 million ordinary shares to new and existing investors in a private placement for expected gross proceeds of $1.30 billion. We issued dual-currency senior secured notes comprising $1.25 billion of U.S. dollar-denominated notes and €500 million of euro-denominated notes, both issued at par and maturing in 2032. We signed and drew a $1.25 billion add-on to our existing U.S. dollar-denominated term loan B and a €395 million add-on to our existing euro-denominated term loan B, both maturing in 2031. ¹ See Non-GAAP financial measures—Adjusted Operating Income and Adjusted Operating Income Margin below for the definition of Adjusted Operating Income and a reconciliation of operating income to Adjusted Operating Income. ² See Non-GAAP financial measures—Adjusted Earnings per Share below for the definition of Adjusted Earnings per Share and a reconciliation of diluted earnings per share to Adjusted Earnings per Share. ³ “Leverage ratio” as of a reporting date is defined as net debt as of such date divided by adjusted EBITDA for the twelve months ending on such date. “Net debt” is defined as nominal outstanding financial debt and the capitalized value of finance lease obligations, less available cash. “Adjusted EBITDA” is defined as earnings before interest, taxes, depreciation, and amortization, determined on a pro forma basis to include the results of the acquired businesses as if they had been owned throughout the entire twelve-month period, adjusted to exclude transaction-related expense, reorganization-related expense, and equity compensation expense, among other items. In addition, adjusted EBITDA reflects achieved cost savings from reorganizations, as well as certain expected cost savings, in each case as if such savings had been achieved at the beginning of the twelve-month period. These calculations are based on assumptions and are subject to risks and uncertainties. The disclaimer included in Forward-looking statements below applies. It is built on open-source components and automatically selects the appropriate AI model for each task, balancing effectiveness and cost. Available models include a range of self-hosted, open-weight models, which we use for most tasks. For the most complex or highest-stakes tasks—and to supervise less advanced models—we use more expensive, closed-weight models. Our model-agnostic harness keeps us independent of any single third-party vendor. Since the beginning of 2026, we have increased the number of pull requests⁵ per Spooner software engineer more than fourfold while reducing inference cost per pull request by roughly half, and by over 90% from mid-year peak levels. We see potential for further productivity gains as we continue to improve our capabilities in AI. We introduced Diagram, a proprietary AI-powered design tool. Specifically tailored to our workflows, we consider it superior to the third-party tools we were previously using for product design, preparation of slide decks, and other design tasks. Leveraging proprietary technologies and improved processes, we significantly compressed our recruiting time for a few roles without any observed compromise in quality. This should allow us to improve our competitiveness in the acquisition of talent. We commenced recruitment activities in the United States as part of our plan to broaden our presence in the country. ⁵ A “pull request” is a formal proposal to add, modify, or remove code in a shared software repository. We substantially completed subscription pricing and packaging adjustments, migrated AOL’s desktop properties to a new instance of the advertising technology stack, rolled out the new desktop email client to all users, and undertook extensive testing across advertising and user experience, with several experiments showing measurable increases in engagement and advertising yield. Eventbrite. We shipped approximately 30 product improvements during Q3, enhanced event discoverability by integrating with ChatGPT, introduced post-checkout advertising while further improving first-party advertising revenue, started piloting new subscription offerings for consumers and organizers, and reduced cloud infrastructure spend while simultaneously investing in capabilities that will improve technical robustness. Tractive. We completed the reorganization, migrated the business onto our proprietary technologies, reduced customer service backlog by 80% by leveraging automated workflows, introduced automatic walk detection, scratching alerts, and better health insights, launched Dog 6 XL Adventure for larger dogs, expanded distribution by signing five new insurance partners and a leading European supermarket chain, and reduced annualized marketing spend by over $10 million through the elimination of unprofitable campaigns. Vimeo. We continued to modernize the Vimeo experience and expand personalization options. We redesigned the OTT checkout flow, delivering an 11% increase in conversion to subscriptions in early testing, and embedded AI analytics in the enterprise offering. Median video transcoding time fell by 40% from the start to the end of Q3. Together with actions taken earlier in the year, the changes implemented in Q3 are expected to avoid more than $7 million of annual hosting costs. More generally, we continued to improve the competitiveness of our businesses via product innovation. For example, we launched Brightcove Gen 2, which brings together a redesigned web video player, AI-generated live captions and universal translation, and AI-enabled agentic capabilities. At komoot, we introduced live tracking, which better positions the service to be used by running and cycling event organizers. At WeTransfer, we introduced end-to-end encrypted transfers for business customers, further strengthening the product as an enterprise-grade solution. We have executed this strategy for more than a decade and, to date, have never sold a material business. We strive to envision the most successful version of an acquired business, and work to close the gap between its current state and that vision as quickly and completely as possible. The transformation is typically deep and entails reorganizing teams, overhauling technology, redesigning user interfaces, accelerating product development, and enhancing marketing and monetization. AI is often both a central component of our vision for the acquired business and a key tool in implementing the transformation. Our performance is driven by our Platform—comprising our people, proprietary technologies, and proprietary data—and reflects our intense focus on achieving exceptional talent density, cultural strength, and technical capabilities. Bending Spoons' main businesses include Airtable, AOL, Brightcove, Eventbrite, Evernote, Miro, Tractive, Vimeo, and WeTransfer. documents.title: How Bending Spoons buys companies: strategy and track record
documents.text: How Bending Spoons buys companies: strategy and track record Bending Spoons has bought over 50 software businesses, including Evernote and AOL, and is now buying Mailchimp. Its filings show how it picks and runs them. Anubhav Sarker Published: 11/20/2026 Last Updated: 11/20/2026 How Bending Spoons buys companies Bending Spoons has spent 13 years buying software that its owners or backers no longer wanted. It usually lets most of the staff go and keeps the product. Its own filings show how the deals get done and who pays for them. On November 19, Intuit told investors it was selling Mailchimp. The email marketing service had cost Intuit about $12 billion in 2021, roughly half in cash and half in shares . The buyer is paying $3.68 billion. Intuit will take $368 million of that in the buyer's stock. The buyer is Bending Spoons , a Milan-based company that began in 2013 with $40,000 left over from a failed diary app. Its first acquisition, an iPhone app for customizing keyboards, cost $10,000 . It has since acquired more than 50 businesses, including Evernote, WeTransfer, Vimeo, AOL, Eventbrite, Airtable and Miro. Mailchimp is the largest purchase it has made, and it follows the pattern of the others. Bending Spoons buys familiar software that has lost favor with its owners or the market, usually at a fraction of its earlier price. It lets most of the staff go, rebuilds the technology on its own tools, changes the pricing, and keeps the business. By its own account , it has never sold a material one. Investors have rewarded it. The company listed on Nasdaq on July 1 at $29 per share and closed that day at $40.50, valuing it at about $25.7 billion. Berkshire Hathaway put $600 million into the offering and another $330 million in October. Revenue was $387 million in 2023. For 2026, the company expects between $3.07 billion and $3.09 billion. Going public meant explaining itself. A prospectus, two quarterly reports and a presentation to bond investors now set out how Bending Spoons chooses targets, what it pays, what it does in the first weeks and how it funds the whole thing. A proxy statement from Eventbrite , which it bought in March, records one negotiation almost day by day. What follows is drawn from those documents, with reporting from named outlets where the filings stop. Figure 1. Sources: company announcements, Bending Spoons prospectus and third-quarter accounts, TechCrunch · five purchases, 2023 to 2026. Each earlier figure is the last funding round, flotation, or sale that put a price on the whole company. A diary app nobody wanted The founding story opens the prospectus , told in the present tense. On a night in August 2010, on the Indonesian island of Lombok, three newly graduated engineers decided to start a company. Francesco Patarnello, Matteo Danieli and Luca Ferrari called it Evertale. The product was a phone app that used AI to write its users' diaries. They raised $1 million and hired 10 people. By the middle of 2013, Evertale had almost no revenue and about four months of cash. They liquidated it, kept the remaining $40,000, and started again with two former colleagues, Luca Querella and Tomasz Greber. The failure produced a theory. Finding a product that people want depends heavily on luck, the founders decided. Running a business well does not. It followed that many products with real customers were probably being run poorly. So the new company would stop inventing products and buy ones that already worked. In the letter's words, it would be "outsourcing the search for product-market fit". Everything else follows from that choice. The founders write that they treated the operating machine as their most important product, ahead of anything it happened to own. The name refers to bending spoons with the mind. A company with $40,000, five people and one failure behind it, the letter says, could use some irony. Its stated models are old-economy acquirers: Henry Singleton at Teledyne and Tom Murphy at Capital Cities, and later Broadcom, Danaher and TransDigm. The second half of the theory is holding on. Bending Spoons says it intends to own what it buys indefinitely, and that when it values a target it largely ignores what the business might fetch in a sale. It gives three reasons never to sell. Nobody else could run the business as profitably. Its engineers rotate between products and would not expect to be sold along with one. And each business is wired so deeply into shared systems that pulling it out would be slow and costly. That is the line it draws between itself and private equity, which buys in order to sell. In other respects the resemblance is close: borrowed money, deep cost cuts and a required rate of return. The record has small exceptions. The prospectus mentions proceeds from the sale of a minor business in 2024 and the disposal of an immaterial one in the first half of 2025. The $10,000 keyboard app was shut down six or seven years ago because too few people used it. The pace has been uneven. More than 10 acquisitions closed in 2017 and none in 2020, when the company built Immuni , Italy's Covid contact-tracing app, without charge. For most of its life, it funded deals with its own cash flow and bank loans. Of the $549 million in new equity it had raised by March 2026, 99% was raised after the start of 2023. That is when the purchases started getting large. A list of 1,000 targets The company has counted its possible targets. Working down from tens of thousands of private and public firms, it says it has found more than 1,000 digital businesses it could plausibly buy over the next few years. Together they took in nearly $400 billion of revenue in 2025. Each makes between $50 million and $5 billion a year, is based in Europe or North America, and earns its money from subscriptions or advertising. Of them, 791 are North American. Few get bought. In 2025, Bending Spoons looked at more than 2,500 opportunities, studied about 200 in depth, and bought six. What gets through is consistent. The prospectus sets four tests. The product must be digital. There must be a lot to improve. The revenue base must be large. And earnings must be predictable several years out, which in practice means customers who stay, little dependence on paid advertising, years of data to study, and a low risk that AI makes the product redundant. Growth is absent from the list. The company describes itself as largely neutral on whether a target is growing, since the expected return determines the decision. Mailchimp's revenue fell 1% to $313 million in its latest quarter. Under these rules, that is no obstacle. Size is on the list because the work does not grow in step with revenue. Ferrari told analysts in August that about 60 of the company's own people worked on Vimeo in the second quarter, roughly as many as rebuilt Evernote in 2023. In the figures in the prospectus, Vimeo's revenue is about four times Evernote's. The return it demands is steep. For deals closed between 2023 and early 2026, the company says it required 25% a year before borrowing and 65% after. The second figure assumes debt of up to 85% of the purchase price, capped at the amount the target's cash flow could repay over five years. The founders' letter concedes that these hurdles may have to fall as the deals get bigger. The valuation routine is designed to stop the buyers fooling themselves. Assumptions are written down as probability ranges across dozens of variables. Nobody may run the model, or look at what it says, until those assumptions are final. The stated reason is to keep people from nudging the inputs towards the price a seller wants. How the Eventbrite deal was negotiated Having set a price, Bending Spoons tends to hold it. The prospectus says the company makes what it considers a compelling offer at the start and is generally unwilling to raise it by much. The proxy statement Eventbrite sent its shareholders shows the policy at work. Ferrari met Julia Hartz, Eventbrite's co-founder and chief executive, at the Allen & Company conference in Sun Valley in July 2024. He described how his company buys things. No deal was discussed. A year later, at the same conference, he proposed one. Five days after that, he sent an email. It named no price. It floated two ideas: that Hartz might put her sale proceeds into Bending Spoons shares, and that she might stay on as chief executive for a fixed period, working beside a senior Bending Spoons manager, with Bending Spoons keeping the final say on the decisions that mattered. On August 22, 2025, Eventbrite's board received an indicative offer of $4.10 to $4.60 a share in cash, with no financing condition. Seven weeks of diligence turned the range into a number: $4.40. The board countered at $5.15. The filing records its view that Bending Spoons had historically been disciplined on price, and its hope that a serious counter might move it. Ferrari answered the same day. There might be a little room, he told Eventbrite's banker, but he would not do a deal at or near $5.15. Nine days later the offer rose to $4.50. Eventbrite's bankers then went looking for someone who would pay more. They approached 13 trade buyers and nine financial ones. Seven signed confidentiality agreements. One bid, at $4.25; declined to go higher. The board signed on December 1 at $4.50, which Bending Spoons had described as its best and final price. The price had moved by $0.10 since October. For shareholders, the price was 81% above the last close of $2.49. For anyone who had held since the 2018 flotation , which valued Eventbrite at $1.76 billion, it was a sale at about $500 million. Hartz did not stay. The filing says she would have no role after closing. She was offered the chance to buy Bending Spoons shares with her after-tax proceeds, at the valuation of its last funding round. Her request to roll her share options over on tax-favorable terms was refused. One detail explains the hurry at the end. Bending Spoons wanted the deal announced before it went to lenders for a new term loan at the start of December. Who it buys from The sellers sort into three kinds. Some are corporate parents shedding a unit: Intuit with Mailchimp, Yahoo with AOL, IAC with a bundle of mobile apps it called Mosaic. Some are listed companies whose shares had sunk. Brightcove, Vimeo and Eventbrite were all taken private. Eventbrite's buyer paid 81% over the market price and still got the company for less than a third of its flotation value. And some are venture-backed companies that were priced for a boom that ended. Miro raised money in January 2022 at a $17.5 billion valuation. Bending Spoons bought it this October for an equity value of about $1.79 billion. Airtable was worth about $11.7 billion to its backers in December 2021 , including the $735 million they had put in, and was sold for about $2.25 billion. Evernote, valued at $1 billion in 2012, went for $199.7 million. Some sellers now take part of the price in Bending Spoons shares. Miro's former shareholders put $295 million back in. Intuit will hold $368 million. The company expects the supply of sellers to improve. Its prospectus argues that AI leaves many single-product software firms exposed, and that this could make their owners readier to sell, at lower prices. The spending has compounded. Bending Spoons closed one deal in 2023, Evernote, at an enterprise value of $194 million. In 2024 it closed five for $876 million, and in 2025 six for $1.92 billion. This year AOL, Eventbrite, Tractive, Airtable and Miro have closed for a combined $5.4 billion. Mailchimp, at $3.68 billion, is due early next year. Figure 2. Enterprise value of acquisitions by year of closing, with 2026 shown deal by deal. Mailchimp is agreed but not closed. Sources: Bending Spoons prospectus, second- and third-quarter 2026 results, deal announcements. What happens after a deal The work starts before the deal closes. As closing nears, the prospectus says, Bending Spoons assembles a task force of its own staff, usually dozens of them, covering engineering, data science, design, product, and growth. Most have done it before on another product. After closing, they spend a few weeks to a few months inside the business, often talking one-on-one with most of the people who work there, reading the code, and interviewing customers. Then they write a plan: a new organization chart, a list of technical fixes, a product roadmap, and a set of pricing and marketing experiments. The organization chart is where the controversy lies. The company's risk disclosures say it has frequently cut staff after acquisitions and expects to do so after each one. It calls its own people Spooners, hires them through a separate and highly selective process, and moves them between products at short notice. The staff who arrive with an acquisition are a different category. Most do not stay. The prospectus gives numbers. Evernote had 341 full-time equivalent staff when it was acquired in January 2023. By the end of 202,4 it had 60, nearly all of them Spooners. Four layers of management became two. StreamYard went from 154 to 44 in under a year, and head office absorbed almost all of its administrative work. Remini came with no team at all. At WeTransfer, the company confirmed to TechCrunch in September 2024 that it planned to cut 75% of its workforce, which TechCrunch, citing Dutch media, put at more than 350. Ferrari explained that the company determines what an acquired business should become, then closes the gap as quickly and as fully as it can. The largest case is the latest one the filings quantify. AOL, Eventbrite and Vimeo brought 1,830 full-time-equivalent staff between them in late 2025 and early 2026. The prospectus says many had already gone by March, and that only a few hundred would remain once the three overhauls were finished later in the year. At Vimeo, a layoff was announced on January 20, eight weeks after closing. At Airtable, the cuts came on October 12, less than six weeks after closing. A Bending Spoons product executive, Federico Simionato, said they reflected the company's belief that small teams ship more, and better, work. Figure 3. Full-time-equivalent staff at purchase and after reorganization. The WeTransfer after-figure is arithmetic from the planned 75% cut. No later figures have been published for AOL, Eventbrite, and Vimeo—sources: Bending Spoons prospectus, TechCrunch. The company says departing staff get substantial support, and the accounts put a price on it. Reorganization costs, mostly separation packages, were $14 million in 2023, $52 million in 2024, and $79 million in 2025. In the first nine months of 2026, they came to $152 million. What replaces the departed is a small team and a lot of shared machinery. The acquired product is moved onto Bending Spoons' own systems for data, payments, and experiments. One estimates what each user will be worth over time. Another handles billing and price changes, allowing the company to take subscription management away from outside vendors soon after a deal closes. The experiment system ran more than 3,000 tests across the portfolio in 2025. AI has made the small teams smaller. The company estimates that the share of its code changes written or co-written by AI went from under 10% in early 2025 to more than 90% a year later. Revenue per Spooner was $1.12 million in 2023 and $2.57 million in 2025. Ferrari said in August that it was running at over $4 million per year. The same standard applies to its own people. In 2025, Bending Spoons received about 800,000 job applications and hired 286. Some 16% of Spooners left that year, and the company says it wanted all but a sliver of those departures. Its filing states plainly that it parts with staff who are performing adequately when it thinks stronger ones are available. What changes for customers Pricing changes early. At Evernote, the company opened every feature to free users, then limited how much of the product they could use. TechCrunch reported that the free tier was cut to 50 notes in November 2023. By the company's count, upgrades triggered by hitting a limit roughly doubled between 2022 and 2024, and revenue per active user in 2025 was two and a half times its 2022 level. The prospectus is candid about the other side of that. Evernote's revenue rose in 2024 because each subscriber paid more, though the number of subscribers declined. WeTransfer's free plan was capped at 10 transfers a month in December 2024, within five months of the purchase. At StreamYard, an automated system now looks for individual accounts that behave like businesses and moves them to business plans. The products do change. Evernote's releases rose by half in 2023 and doubled in 2024. The company fixed more than 6,000 reliability problems in three years and redesigned the apps. New sign-ups had fallen by about a fifth in each of the three years to 2023. They rose 29% in 2024 and 20% in 2025. Remini, a photo app bought in 2021, made more than nine times as much revenue in 2025 as it had before the purchase. In October, the company gave bond investors an average across the deals it has done since 2023. Six quarters after purchase, revenue was 32% higher, and adjusted operating costs were 59% lower. Those two numbers are the business. What the accounts show Revenue was $387 million in 2023, $671 million in 2024, and $1.31 billion in 2025. In the third quarter of 2026 alone, it was $780 million. Nearly all of that growth was bought. The company reports what its businesses would have done without new acquisitions, a figure it calls organic growth. It was 7% in 2024 and 13% in 2025. In the three quarters of 2026 reported so far, it was 6%, 3% and 3%, against headline growth of more than 120% each time. Figure 4.Year-on-year revenue growth, reported and organic. Ferrari told analysts in August that Remini and Splice had declined in the second quarter. Brightcove lost subscribers in 2025. The strongest contributors lately have been WeTransfer and Tractive, a pet tracker bought in May. Profit depends on which line you read. The company's preferred measure, adjusted operating income, excludes the amortization of acquisition costs, deal fees, and reorganization costs. On that basis, it made $613 million in 2025, a margin of 47%. Operating income under standard accounting was $278 million. After $143 million in interest and a tax charge swelled by the relocation of acquired businesses to Italy, the year ended with a net loss of $204,000. Figure 5. From adjusted operating income to net income, 2025. Source: Bending Spoons prospectus. The case for the adjusted figure is that severance and deal fees are one-off costs. The case against is that a company which buys something every few months pays them every few months. This year the gap has narrowed. Net income for the first nine months of 2026 was $295 million, according to the third-quarter results. Debt and funding The purchases are paid for mostly with debt. Borrowings stood at $389 million at the end of 2023, $2.67 billion at the end of 2025, and $4.91 billion this September. The October presentation to bond investors, which includes the Miro purchase and related financing around it, shows gross debt of $6.64 billion against $1.52 billion in cash. Figure 6. Debt and cash at reporting dates, December 2023 to September 2026. The October 2026 bond sale and the Miro purchase are not included. Sources: Bending Spoons prospectus, second- and third-quarter 2026 results. It is not cheap money. The main dollar loan costs about 9.2% a year after hedging. In November, the company sold its first bonds : $1.25 billion at 9.625% and €500 million at 8.625%, both due in 2032. Interest expense was $17 million in 2023 and $143 million in 2025. In the second quarter of 2026 alone, it was $109 million. The company puts its leverage at 2.1 times earnings, comfortably within the 4.0 limit set by its lenders. The definition matters. The earnings in that ratio count each acquired business as if it had been owned all year and include cost savings, both those already realized and those still expected. In the 12 months to June, the bond presentation shows, $505 million of the $2.26 billion total was savings the company expected but had not yet delivered. New shares are issued sparingly. Before the flotation, the company had raised $549 million of fresh equity in its whole history. The July IPO raised $1.10 billion for the company after fees, with existing shareholders selling stock alongside the company. On the day it agreed to buy Mailchimp, it also arranged to sell 32.5 million new shares to institutional investors at $40 per share. Control has barely been diluted. The four co-founders still at the company hold shares that each carry five votes. After the IPO, the prospectus shows, they had about 83% of the votes between them. One more disclosure deserves notice. The prospectus reports material weaknesses in the company's financial controls. The fixes it lists include better controls over unusual transactions and over the integration of newly acquired businesses into its reporting. Criticism and risks The people who lose their jobs have the plainest objection. After Vimeo cut a former engineer, Derek Buitenhuis, wrote that it hurt to see something he had built destroyed by what he called "private equity dressed up as a technology company." Founders have complained too. Nalden, who co-founded WeTransfer in 2009, criticized what had become of it last December and is building a rival file-transfer service. Bending Spoons does not hide from this in its filings. It warns investors that reorganizations and price increases may damage its brands, and that a reputation for layoffs could make owners reluctant to sell to it. It discloses that it has faced employment claims connected to reorganizations. Its defense is the customer numbers. Net revenue retention across the portfolio was 95% in 2025. At Evernote, it averaged 99% over three years. Nearly half of subscription revenue comes from customers of at least five years' standing. Matteo Danieli, a co-founder, told TechCrunch on the day of the listing that retention had been remarkably stable through the price changes. The company has also told bond investors that it has never lost money on a material acquisition. The same numbers allow a less flattering reading. A retention rate of 95% means that revenue from existing customers shrinks by 5% a year before any new ones arrive. And the customers who stay longest are often the ones who would find it hardest to go. The prospectus says as much about Evernote, which it valued partly because many users had thousands of notes stored there and had built their working habits around it. The company's own list of risks is long. The growth is acquired, so it slows if the deals slow. The deals need debt at 9% or more. The teams that do the overhauls are finite: about 700 Spooners are absorbing five businesses bought this year, and Ferrari said in August that he could not rule out having to slow the buying from time to time. Large targets are also scarce. Of the more than 1,000 companies on its list, 94 have revenue above $1 billion. What's next? Mailchimp is a different order of purchase. At $3.68 billion, it is more than twice the size, by enterprise value, of anything Bending Spoons has bought before. It brings in about $1.26 billion a year, close to the revenue of Bending Spoons' total revenue in 2025. The price is about 2.9 times that revenue. The arithmetic of the model is simple. Buy at two or three times revenue. Take out more than half the costs. Raise prices where customers will bear it and keep most of them. A business bought with 9% money can then return a great deal more than 9%. Evernote suggests it works: bought for $199.7 million, it produced $95 million in revenue and $11 million in pre-tax profit in its first year, which also included $14 million in severance. Each step leans on something the company does not control. Sellers have to keep accepting low prices, which they have done during a slump in software valuations. Lenders have to keep lending. Customers have to keep tolerating the price changes. And about 700 people have to keep absorbing businesses several times larger than the last. Three numbers are worth watching. The first is organic growth, which was 3% last quarter. If it turns negative, the portfolio is shrinking underneath the acquisitions. The second is the gap between the cost savings the company expects and those it has delivered, which indicates whether the overhauls are keeping up with the buying. The third is the price of its debt, because the model needs a wide spread between what it pays lenders and what it earns on deals. The founders have already told investors that the return they demand on new deals may have to fall. Bending Spoons would say none of this is new, and 13 years of results support it. But the record was built on smaller deals.
